lignes.texte: ChatGPT is nothing but hype. It might be portrayed as the
greatest technology breakthrough, but it’s really, it’s a financial hostage situation.
Every single day, OpenAI is burning through cash. Billions of dollars are going up in smoke trying
to keep the AI dream alive. And the industry knows it. If OpenAI fails, the rest go down with it.
Sam Altman has literally forced Big Tech into a corner.
But OpenAI isn’t limiting their spending. They’re doubling down. A stealth corporate restructuring
is going to land firmly in your pocket. And there’s nothing you can do to stop it.
The crisis isn’t coming. It’s already here.
Every week, more than 900 million people type something into ChatGPT.
They ask it to fix code, plan meals, and even settle arguments about history. By almost any
measure, it’s one of the most successful consumer products ever built, costing users around $20 each
month for the latest model. And yet, the company
behind it operates at a massive loss. In June 2026, audited figures showed OpenAI
was growing at a pace almost nobody has ever seen… while losing money at a pace nobody has ever seen.
In 2025, revenue jumped from $3.7 billion to $13.07 billion. Tripling sales in a single year
would be the highlight of a decade for most. But that’s not the case with OpenAI.
Total costs and expenses that same year reached $34 billion, leaving an operating
loss of $20.92 billion. PFor every dollar ChatGPT and its sister products brought in,
OpenAI spent roughly $2.60 to earn it. The bottom-line number looks even worse.
OpenAI’s net hit $38.53 billion. Some of that is just accounting paperwork
and no real cash left the building, but the real world damage is terrifying.
They ran a $21 billion operating deficit. Defenders like to say OpenAI is following
the Amazon playbook: lose money now to dominate the market later. But look at the scale. Amazon’s
worst single-year net loss was $1.4 billion. OpenAI’s operating loss alone was about 15
times that. One analyst commented that no startup in history has ever operated with
losses anywhere close to this size. And that financial hole isn’t
closing anytime soon. A Deutsche Bank analysis
said OpenAI is expected to hemorrhage $143 billion by2029. Right now, they’re sitting on
$50 billion in assets, nearly half of it in cash. But at this burn rate, that won’t last long.
And losses like that don’t just disappear. Someone has to pay for them.
In October 2025, OpenAI underwent a corporate mutation. It shed its non-profit identity
and became a massive for profit juggernaut. It was a long way from where it all started.
OpenAI was founded in 2015, with Elon Musk and Sam Altman as co-chairs. Its mission
was to make sure advanced AI benefited all of humanity, not a handful of shareholders.
But building cutting-edge AI turned out to be insanely expensive, and a charity can’t sell
stock to raise tens of billions of dollars. So in 2019, the mission gave way to money.
And the blowblack almost exploded in November 2023, when OpenAI’s board abruptly fired Sam
Altman as CEO. Within days, hundreds of employees threatened to mutiny and follow him to Microsoft.
Altman was reinstated, the board was purged and the financial brakes were cut immediately.
Two years later, before the public ever got a chance to buy in, the people closest to
the company orchestrated a historic payday. In October 2025, with the company losing more
money, OpenAI employees sold about $6.6 billion of stock to private investors. The deal was
valued at $500 billion, making it the world’s most valuable startup at the time. Just months earlier,
during a SoftBank-led round, it had been valued at $300 billion. Around
600 employees walked away with $11 million each. While it’s totally legal, the timeline is suspect.
The insiders cashed out at the peak. Anyone buying in next is left holding the bag.
Which raises an obvious question. Why would investors keep paying more
for a company that keeps losing more? At $500 billion, OpenAI was valued at
roughly 25 times its projected annual revenue. Most established software companies trade at
somewhere between 5 and 15 times. The answer is that investors weren’t paying for what OpenAI
earned. They were paying for what they believed it would become: the company that builds the most
powerful AI first, and then owns the market. In AI, that comes with a price tag.
To build a better model, you need to throw more computing power at it. That
means every jump in valuation isn’t just for show. It’s the fuel OpenAI needs to
raise its next multi-billion dollar round of cash. When SoftBank-led valued OpenAI at $300 billion,
it wasn’t just paper wealth. It came with a demand to pour another $40 billion
straight into infrastructure. In other words, the valuation
and the spending aren't two separate stories. And the numbers are spiraling out of control.
In 2025, OpenAI’s research and development spending reached $19.18 billion. Sales and
marketing jumped more than fivefold, to $5.73 billion. And OpenAI handed Microsoft $17.2 billion
for research, infrastructure, and other costs. Microsoft paid OpenAI $303 million in return.
And here’s the fatal flaw of AI. With traditional software, serving
one more customer costs practically nothing. But every single ChatGPT answer runs on expensive
chips inside power-hungry data centers. More users means more revenue, but it also means
more servers, more electricity, more cooling, and more chips, which feeds back into costs.
To feed this demand, OpenAI went nuclear. Literally.
In September 2025, OpenAI committed to building at least 10 gigawatts of AI data centers running on
Nvidia systems. That’s roughly the output of 10 large nuclear reactors. And according to NVIDIA
CEO Jensen Huang, building just one gigawatt of AI data center capacity costs up to $60 billion.
By late 2025, OpenAI had racked up around $1.4 trillion in data center and computing commitments.
They made $70 in long-term promises for every dollar in revenue they brought in.
Internal projections show the company expects to spend around $856 billion
on computing power and infrastructure by the end of 2030 alone. That’s larger than
the annual GDP of almost every country on Earth. No company can pay for that out of its own pocket.
This is where the story gets strange. Imagine you run a hardware store. A contractor
walks in wanting to build a mansion, but he can’t afford the materials. So you lend him the money,
on one condition: every dollar has to be spent in your store. He buys
your lumber with your cash, and at the end of the quarter, you report record sales.
That’s what’s happening at the center of the AI boom.
In September 2025, NVIDIA announced plans to invest up to $100 billion in OpenAI,
released in stages as OpenAI switched on new Nvidia-powered data centers.
The first $10 billion would arrive when the first gigawatt came online.
Around the same time, OpenAI agreed to spend $300 billion on Oracle’s
cloud services. Oracle’s stock soared 36% in a single day, adding $251 billion in market value.
But Oracle can’t run that cloud without NVIDIA chips, so it has to buy them from Nvidia.
So NVIDIA invests in OpenAI. OpenAI pays Oracle. Oracle buys from NVIDIA. After going around in
that circle, the money ends up right back in NVIDIA’s pocket. And along the way,
the same cash shows up as growth at all 3 companies at once: chip revenue
at NVIDIA, a booming order backlog at Oracle, and infrastructure backing OpenAI’s growth forecasts.
And OpenAI isn’t the only AI company abusing the loop.
By 2026, analysts had identified more than $800 billion in these kinds of circular arrangements
across the AI supply chain. Even OpenAI’s biggest competitor, Anthropic is using a similar structure
with Google and Amazon to create funding seemingly out of nowhere. Then in July 2026,
the Wall Street Journal reported that NVIDIA was in talks to guarantee roughly
$250 billion in financing for a 10-gigawatt campus being developed in southern Ohio.
But why would the world’s most valuable chipmaker need to vouch for one of its largest AI customers?
Because OpenAI doesn’t have an investment-grade credit rating. Lenders price loans on a borrower’s
ability to pay. A company losing more than $20 billion a year doesn’t look great on paper.
To bypass this, Nvidia stepped in as the ultimate financial safety net. An SEC filing
disclosed that Nvidia is guaranteeing the land, power, and buildings for about 4.25
gigawatts at the Ohio site, which will host NVIDIAup to $105 billion to cover the land,
power and buildings for OpenAIs data centers. But that’s just for real estate. The chips going
inside could reach another $350 billion. If this sounds familiar, it should.
In the late 1990s, tech giants like Lucent, Nortel and Cisco lent billions to cash strapped internet
start ups so they could buy gear. When the dot-com bubble burst, the start ups went under, the loans
went bad, and the tech vendors’ went with them. NVIDIA is a far stronger company than Lucent
ever was. Its data center business alone brought in $193.7 billion in 2026. But the
structure is similar. The supplier’s fortunes and the customer’s ability to pay are now tied
together. If OpenAI can’t cover its rent, NVIDIA loses its biggest customer and inherits the bill.
And that bill doesn’t stop at NVIDIA’s front door. It has at least four ways of reaching you.
The first might be your retirement account, since most traditional 401(k)s and Roth
IRAs bet on the same thing: the S&P 500. And AI has become a large part of that.
In its October 2025 quarterly filing, Microsoft revealed that losses from its OpenAI investment
slashed its net income by $3.1 billion in a single quarter. That knocked 41 cents off
its earnings per share. Without OpenAI, they would have been about 11% higher.
And it works in both directions. When private AI companies raise cash
at higher valuations, their investors book paper gains straight into their profits. In early 2026,
S&P 500 earnings grew by around 48%. But strip out the paper AI gains from Big Tech,
and the true market growth drops to closer to 29%. This all matters because of how top-heavy the
stock market has become. By late 2025, the top 10 companies in the S&P 500 are involved in AI or
software in some way. Several of the S&P 500’s largest companies are heavily exposed to AI.
NVIDIA, Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Broadcom Meta and Tesla are all locked in.
So when OpenAI’s valuation goes up, a big part of the index gets a lift. But if OpenAI stumbles,
the shockwave wipes out the savings of millions of ordinary investors who never even went in on AI.
The second way is one you’ll see in your mailbox every month.
Your electricity bill. AI data centers use staggering
amounts of electricity, but the grid was never built for them. PJM, the operator that runs the
largest wholesale power market in North America, serves around 65 million customers across 13
states and Washington, D.C. And demand keeps climbing.
By 2030, PJM projects summer demand will be about 30 gigawatts higher than in 2025,
much of it from data centers. That’s like adding several large cities’ worth of
power demand to the grid in just 5 years. Every year, PJM holds an auction to make
sure there will be enough power capacity in the future. For the 2024-25 period, the price was
$28.92 per megawatt-day. For 2026-27, it cleared at $329.17, a more than tenfold jump. PJM’s own
independent market monitor found that data centers were responsible for 63% of the price increase.
The Natural Resources Defense Council estimates that PJM consumers could pay an extra $163 billion
through 2033 to cover the difference. OpenAI isn’t the sole culprit.
Every major tech company is racing to build data centers. But OpenAI is building at a scale almost
nobody else can match, and its flagship center in Ohio sits squarely inside PJM territory.
The backlash has already started. In July 2026, New York placed a one-year
moratorium on new data center construction, the first statewide ban of its kind. Other
states are trying to claw back the tax breaks they handed out to attract these projects.
And when a family pays more for electricity to keep an AI campus running, they don’t get a share
of the data center. They just get the bill. The third way is the one OpenAI has tried
hardest to deny: taxes. On November 5th, 2025,
OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar dropped a massive bombshell at a Wall Street Journal event. She suggested a
government guarantee could make financing their AI chips much cheaper and let the company borrow
more. When the interviewer asked whether she meant a taxpayer backstop, she agreed.
The public uproar was instant. That same night, Friar backpeddled
on LinkedIn, saying “OpenAI is not seeking a government backstop.” The next day,
White House AI czar David Sacks said there would be no federal bailout for AI, while Sam Altman
insisted that taxpayers should not bail out “companies that make bad business decisions.”
Sacks added that the U.S. had at least 5 major frontier AI companies,
so no single AI lab was too big to fail. But Altman’s statement had a caveat.
Shortly before those comments,OpenAI had lobbied the White House to extend chip-manufacturing tax
credits to AI data centers. They suggested the government “should deploy grants, cost-sharing
agreements, loans, or loan guarantees.” Senator Elizabeth Warren sounded the alarm,
warning of a pattern America has seen before: companies take on huge debt, make risky bets,
and then demand a taxpayer bailout when those bets go south. In January 2026, she wrote to
Altman directly, flagging partners like CoreWeave that are loaded with debt to fulfill their OpenAI
contracts, meanwhile OpenAI itself carries comparatively little debt on its own books.
In other words, the borrowing is everyone else’s problem.
Then, in July 2026, Altman launched his ultimate play. He proposed giving the U.S. government a
5% stake in the company, worth about $42.6 billion. Altman’s pitch was that it would
let ordinary Americans share in AI’s upside. Other leading AI developers, including Google,
Meta and Anthropic, would be asked to do the same. It’s not a fringe idea, either. Even Senator
Bernie Sanders has pushed for the public to take a 50% stake in AI companies.
On paper, a public stake sounds generous. But in practice, it’s a Trojan Horse. Once the government
owns 5% of OpenAI, a collapse is no longer just a private loss. It’s a loss on a public asset
held in the name of every American. OpenAI isn’t sharing the upside, it’s pre-selling the downside.
Then there’s the fourth way: the collapse of your retirement fund.
On June 8th, 2026, OpenAI took its first steps to going public by confidentially submitting
a draft S-1 to the SEC. While Sam Atlman confirmed they wouldn’t go public in 2026,
a 2027 listing is looking likely. And when it does arrive, the rules of the
market have been rewritten to snare your money. In 2026, Nasdaq introduced a “fast entry” rule.
Any newly listed companies big enough to rank among the top 40 members of the Nasdaq-100 can
be forced into the index within 15 trading days of their IPO. They don’t have to wait
the standard 3 months. The S&P500 and FTSE Russell are making similar moves.
This is important because more than $30 trillion in global wealth tracks these indexes. The moment
OpenAI goes public and uses the fast lane, index funds and private pension accounts will become
automatic buyers of OpenAI stock. Whether you want to or not.
The early investors and insiders who got in at lower prices finally have
someone to sell to. And if OpenAI does collapse, so will the retirement funds.
None of this means OpenAI is doomed. Back in 2019, before ChatGPT existed,
Sam Altman joked that OpenAI had no plans to make revenue. Once it built a truly intelligent system,
it would simply ask the AI how to generate returns for investors. 7 years later,
the company brings in billions of dollars and serves close to a billion people a week.
If OpenAI really does hit $350 billion in annual revenue by 2030, today’s losses will
look like one of the boldest investments in business history. Everyone holding a piece of
it will be glad they did. But the size of the bet
has changed who’s making it. This is no longer a handful of
venture capitalists rolling the dice on a startup. It’s chipmakers guaranteeing leases, cloud giants
booking paper profits, utilities passing costs to households, a government being offered a stake,
and index funds waiting to buy in on Day 15. Every one of those players
has a reason to believe. NVIDIA sells more chips. Oracle
and Microsoft fill their data centers. Insiders have already cashed out once. Governments get a
seat at the table of the most important technology of the century. The only group that never really
got asked is the one at the end of the line. OpenAI burns the cash. Big Tech funds the
lifeline. And if the numbers don’t come through, the people left holding the bill won’t be the ones
who wrote the business plan. They’ll be the ones with a 401(k), an electric bill, and a tax return.
So the real question isn’t whether OpenAI can build the future. It’s
who pays for it if the future arrives late. As the AI arms race accelerates, the world's
most powerful models are suddenly putting hard limits on how much you can use them. Watch “Why
is OpenAI so Unprofitable” to find out why the industry is hitting a wall. Or click on this.
